citation: ABI Code of Practice for the Categorisation of Motorised Vehicle Salvage (28 May 2025)
title: Salvage categories A/B/S/N, the Appropriately Qualified Person, MIAFTR and the EV/high-voltage battery rules
principle: The May 2025 Code keeps four categories — A (scrap/recycle, must be crushed), B (break for parts, body shell crushed), S (repairable, structural damage) and N (repairable, non-structural damage) — and requires every categorisation to be made by an Appropriately Qualified Person who takes responsibility for the final decision in a dispute, with DVLA notification and MIAFTR recording for each category. The 2025 revision brings electric and hybrid vehicles within scope with specific guidance for high-voltage (over 60V) batteries including structural battery designs where the battery forms part of the chassis, and addresses megacasting and reusable parts. CCGUK records the category, the AQP and the source; it does not write to MIAFTR. A Cat S/N marker depresses PAV and must be disclosed in comparables.

citation: Lay Representatives (Rights of Audience) Order 1999, SI 1999/1225, art 2
title: Any person may address the court in a small claims hearing — but not if the client does not attend, after judgment, or on appeal
principle: In proceedings dealt with as a small claim any person may exercise rights of audience in accordance with rules of court, except that a lay representative may not do so where the client does not attend the hearing, at any stage after judgment, or on an appeal against the district judge's decision. CPR 27.14(3) applies the small claims costs caps to any fee charged by a lay representative. This is CCGUK's only lawful route to speak in court: the claimant must be present, and CCGUK must not conduct the litigation (Legal Services Act 2007 s.12).
text: A lay representative may not exercise any right of audience— (a) where his client does not attend the hearing; (b) at any stage after judgment; or (c) on any appeal brought against any decision made by the district judge in the proceedings.

citation: ICO data protection fee — Data Protection (Charges and Information) Regulations 2018 as amended 2025
title: ICO fee: tier 1 £52 (turnover up to £632,000 or no more than 10 staff); tier 2 £78; tier 3 £3,763; £5 Direct Debit discount
principle: Every controller must pay the annual data protection fee unless exempt. Tier 1 (micro organisations: turnover up to £632,000 or 10 or fewer staff) is £52; tier 2 (turnover up to £36m or 250 or fewer staff) is £78; otherwise tier 3 at £3,763; paying by Direct Debit deducts £5. CCGUK is tier 1. Settings must hold the ICO registration number and renewal date; failure to pay attracts a fixed penalty.

citation: DVLA form V888 — request by an individual for information about a vehicle
title: DVLA keeper enquiry: £2.50 for the registered keeper at the date of an event (reasonable cause); £5 for further information
principle: A person with reasonable cause (including finding out who was responsible for an accident, tracing the keeper of an abandoned or illegally parked vehicle, or suspected insurance fraud) may apply on form V888 for the name and address of the registered keeper at a specific date for £2.50; further information such as a copy document or additional keeper history costs £5 per vehicle. Companies use V888/2 or V888X2A. Record the reasonable-cause statement on the claim file before applying.

citation: MIB askMID "Other Vehicle Look-up" (to be rebranded "Check Their Vehicle")
title: askMID one-off search for the other vehicle's insurer: £10.00, non-refundable; annual subscription for claims handlers
principle: A party involved in an accident can run a one-off askMID search on the other vehicle's registration and accident date for £10.00 (non-refundable); if found, the insurer name, policy number and claims contact details are returned on screen. Organisations such as solicitors and claims handling companies can take an annual subscription. MIB has said askMID is being replatformed and rebranded "Check Their Vehicle" — watch the URL. Misuse (searching vehicles not involved in an accident with the enquirer) is prohibited.

citation: Metropolitan Police General Fees and Charges 2026 — Forms 518 and 519

citation: TfL private hire vehicle licensing — zero emission capable requirement (from 1 January 2023)
title: Every vehicle licensed as a London PHV for the first time must be zero emission capable and Euro 6
principle: Since 1 January 2023 all private hire vehicles licensed by TfL for the first time, whatever their age, must be zero emission capable and meet Euro 6; TfL's PHV definition requires CO2 of no more than 75g/km with a zero-emission range of at least 20 miles (the stricter 50g/km alternative in the blueprint was not returned by TfL pages and should be checked), and vehicles must be no older than 10 years at re-licensing. Neither current CCGUK unit qualifies for first licensing, so the PCO plan needs a ZEC vehicle; the fleet module should block "PCO" class-of-use allocation for non-ZEC units.

citation: MIB Uninsured Drivers Agreement 2015 (England, Scotland and Wales) and MIB claims guidance
title: Uninsured driver claims: limitation-based time limits (3 years personal injury; 6 years property damage), claim via the MIB portal
principle: Where the at-fault driver is identified but uninsured, the claim is made to MIB under the 2015 Agreement (new claims via the online portal). MIB states a personal injury claim must be received within three years of the accident and a property damage claim within six years (England and Wales), mirroring the Limitation Act. The Agreement contains conditions precedent (notice of proceedings, cooperation, assignment of judgment) that must be checked against the Agreement text before issuing against an uninsured driver; MIB reports an average claim window of around nine months. Injury elements are referred out.

citation: MIB Untraced Drivers Agreement 2017 and MIB claims guidance
title: Hit-and-run (untraced driver) claims: report to the police within 14 days; 3 years personal injury / 6 years property damage
principle: Where the driver cannot be traced, compensation is sought from MIB under the 2017 Agreement. MIB's guidance requires the incident to have been reported to the police within 14 days (even if the claim is submitted later) and the claim to be made within three years for personal injury and six years for property damage; MIB investigates and decides the application itself (no court claim against a defendant). Check the Agreement text for the property-damage conditions and any excess before advising a client; the police reference and report date are mandatory evidence fields.

title: Stopping distances and following gap — the rear-end collision rule
principle: A driver must drive at a speed that allows stopping well within the distance seen to be clear, leave enough space to pull up safely if the vehicle in front slows or stops, never get closer than the overall stopping distance, and allow at least a two-second gap (doubled on wet roads, up to ten times on ice). In a rear-end shunt the following driver is presumptively at fault; the lead driver's sudden stop rarely displaces this.
text: Drive at a speed that will allow you to stop well within the distance you can see to be clear. ... Leave enough space between you and the vehicle in front so that you can pull up safely if it suddenly slows down or stops. The safe rule is never to get closer than the overall stopping distance.

title: Before moving off: mirrors, blind spots, signal, do not pull out into the path of others

title: Do not overtake where you might come into conflict: junctions, narrowing roads, forcing others to swerve
principle: Drivers must not overtake where they might come into conflict with other road users — approaching or at a junction, where the road narrows, approaching crossings, where another road user would be forced to swerve or slow down, or when a vehicle ahead is indicating or slowing to turn. title: Road junctions: look all round before emerging; emerge only into a safe gap

title: Roundabouts: give priority to traffic approaching from the right
principle: On reaching a roundabout a driver must give priority to traffic approaching from the right unless signs, markings or lights direct otherwise, check whether markings allow entry without giving way, watch for traffic already on the roundabout (especially those intending to leave by the next exit), and look right before joining. title: Roundabouts: signals and lane position for left, straight ahead and right exits
principle: Taking the first exit: signal left and approach in the left-hand lane, keep left and keep signalling. Taking a right exit or going full circle: select the appropriate lane on approach, normally no signal on approach, stay in lane until needing to alter course, signal left after passing the exit before the one wanted. Intermediate exits: select the appropriate lane, normally no signal on approach, signal left after passing the exit before the one wanted. Lane-discipline and exit-signal failures on roundabouts are apportioned using this rule.
text: When taking the first exit to the left, unless signs or markings indicate otherwise signal left and approach in the left-hand lane; keep to the left on the roundabout and continue signalling left to leave ... signal left after you have passed the exit before the one you want.
